newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Tide turns against Afghan Taleban north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Tide turns against Afghan Taleban north of Kabul.

text.p: The tide has turned sharply against the purist Islamic Taleban militia north of Kabul, but it is far from clear that the government it ousted two weeks ago is in a position to retake the Afghan capital, analysts said on Sunday.

"We are seeing that the Taleban magic doesn't work north of Kabul, but whether the former government can roll back the carpet all the way to Kabul depends on a host of factors," one veteran Afghan watcher said.

Just five days ago, the forces of ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood were bottled up in his Panjsher Valley fortress, to which he withdrew as the Taleban took Kabul and set about imposing stern Islamic Sharia law on the liberal city.

The Tajik chief had sealed the narrow entrance to the valley with landslides. Although the mostly ethnic Pushtun Taleban made little headway in their noisy assault, Masood appeared entirely on the defensive.

Then, with a military alliance with northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum nearing completion, Masood launched a surprise counter-attack in the Salang Pass that leads through the Hindu Kush mountains to Uzbek territory.

The attack forced the Taleban to break off their attempt to get into the Panjsher and Masood pressed his Salang attack down to Jabal-os-Siraj, the headquarters town for both fronts at the mouth of the pass.
Next, he started guerrilla attacks behind the lines, hitting the town of Charikar, a 30-minute drive to the south, and nearby Bagram, the main airbase 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul.

Other local commanders, after what local people said were visits from Masood's envoys, started attacking the Taleban near the entrance to the Kabul valley and cutting the main road north, isolating major concentrations of Taleban forces.
"These were exactly the tactics Masood used against the Soviet army in the 1980s," when Moscow backed a communist government in Kabul, another Afghan watcher said.
"They worked then and they are working now. The Taleban are very badly rattled."

That is evident in a radical shift in attitude to western reporters at the front-line. Where once cheerful Taleban fighters happily chatted about what was going on, now they are surly at best and aggressive at worst.
At least two reporters have been beaten just north of Kabul and one who had his camera smashed complained to the Taleban authorities in Kabul. He said he was told he deserved the beating.
Other reporters at the front have been threatened with death.
"It seems the Taleban control little more than the road north and almost nothing on either side of it," said one analyst with a military background.

But he and others said it seemed unlikely Masood -- military chief in the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani -- could attack Kabul in the immediate future without the support of Dostum.
Masood, Dostum and Shia Moslem leader Karim Khalili signed a pact pledging to support each other against the Sunni Moslem Taleban if attacked.

One Taleban minister rejected the idea of a ceasefire and another said the movement which has swept to control of three-quarters of Afghanistan in just two years still wanted to talk peace with Dostum.

"Right now there are no serious signs of talks, but there are no confirmed signs either of Dostum moving militarily to help Dostum," an Afghan watcher said. "Until he does, these guys can't take Kabul."
